### Why do this problem?

This problem invites children to just literally discuss/discuss why they have made an observation and then to go on and be critical and analytical about something that they perceive could be/become problematic if not corrected. There is no effort even to ask a closed question at the end - you have nearly finished the question by the time you get to the end of the first sentence. Curiously, the word 'why' doesn't appear anywhere. Letting children take responsibility for the mathematics serves to enhance the learning environment in the classroom. Having challenging but accessible problems which promote discussion is something all teachers can aspire to and achieve in their own ways. Some further thoughts can be found here.

### Possible approach

Invite a class discussion about the problem itself first, after making your own mathematical notes about what could follow. Invite two children, with different opinions, to articulate their ideas/perspectives together (but don't tell them they must do this together - see below). You may wish to use mini-whiteboards and other resources to represent Jon's thinking whilst the children discuss it. This could be an opportunity to video record as some children may want to refer to their earlier talk later or it could act as an opportunity to have an audio commentary (as a useful assessment tool).

### Key questions

Have we only got two different views on this issue? What are our two main points of view?
What will happen if one child/person 'wins' the discussion?
Can we start again and compare our ideas?
Does Jon understand his own mathematical ideas?
Does Eva understand Jon's mathematical ideas?
Is it enough to say 'you got that wrong' and stop?
Is it enough to say 'no, I didn't'?

### Possible support

Encourage learners to talk in pairs about the two mathematical statements. What do they think of Jon's written mathematical calculation? Where is the inconsistency within the communication? Create a display of mathematical language to have at hand. You could look at Talking Maths in School and this sheet to see the kinds of questions children ask and how their learning progresses.
Make an inter-active activity with unpacking paper.

Make a prediction.
Look very carefully at what the teacher does.

### 27 Symmetry in linguistics (Language, Cambridge)

Patrick Suppes' (1981) view of this area seems typical. For him, it is unreasonable to think that one hypothesis which might decide the question of symmetry could possibly be of any use in attacking other language universals. Innumerable hypotheses can be formulated, and if decades of past experience are any guide, it would be a minor miracle if one all-purpose hypothesis would suffice for all universals.

Suppes has formulated his views with particular care and precision, and thus he has made it clear what is at stake. If his general conclusion is correct, namely that we will usually have to employ special hypothesis - impossible to enumerate in advance - to deal with particular cases, then we have no idea how many genuinely symmetrical language universals exist. We will be in trouble even before we can attempt to answer questions such as “Is it all right to prefer symmetry?”, or “Are symmetrical universals more worthy of pursuit than asymmetrical ones?” These are questions on which both capital N and Kim and some of their critics have much to offer.

In this sense the author's job is similar to that of a lawyer; it is the author's job to discover, interpret and learn from the graphic, documentary and human evidence that might be available. The researcher does not begin by collecting data; he or she begins by finding and understanding what is being done, saying or writing. He or she enters a social setting, tries to "make sense of it, trying to identify both the "comings and goings," of the people and the flow of the activity," then seeks the data that will best reveal that activity. Only then does the researcher begin to "collect data methodically and strategically rather than accidentally (i.e., serendipitously), but it is in the serendipitous and episodic sightings and chance questioning (in natural contexts) that the researcher often starts the "looking, listening and note-taking" that identifies and inspires the best research questions (Green and Wallat, 1981, p. 27). This evidence is not totally controlled by the researcher; events just happen and are gathered by the serendipitous researcher who filters them through his or her questions and concepts.

There would clearly be an error. What kind of error do you think it would be?

Presentation

Did you find a good way of solving the problem? How would you explain your efforts?

If you didn't succeed at first, is there something you would do differently a second time around? Can you find a strategy for proving errors like this in the future?

You don't have to make mistakes to have interesting things happen. If you ask "Suppose we did this," or "Suppose we changed these numbers," you can come up with many different possibilities. Try to look at "what would happen if" as a challenge to think of interesting variations - changes that don't at all change the purpose of the game, but do change what happens in a game!

Storytelling

Make up a problem to share with a friend. Could you do this on a computer game? Could you do this on paper? What changes would you make?

When you eventually have a solution that works for you, do you think it is the best solution? Could somebody improve your system by making a change. Could you use the strategy you used to solve the problem to tackle a harder one? What is the hardest challenge like this you could imagine tackling?

Extension

Differentiate More!

In "Big Numbers" (NCTM News, July 2008), Marjorie Crabtree defined differentiation in terms of using three instructional tiers of pacing, content, and process to match the instruction to the needs of all students. There are many ways to differentiate instruction to support a mathematical productive struggle. Abe Zamansky (secantnerve.blogspot.com) shares presentations that he used in a graduate curriculum design seminar. My favorite is the collaboration/decoration activity he did with his wife over many hours. He wanted pieces of paper with different decorations hanging under a staircase in his apartment. He and his wife took alternating turns applying decorations to the available papers, which he jokingly called "paper arranging," (i.e., randomizing). The purpose of this collaboration/decoration activity was to discuss the nonaccuracy of the words even and odd in elementary school. For example, when labeling multi-digit paper chains as even or odd, the question might be asked, "If the counting numbers represent a chain, which would you like to start on: an even-colored link or an odd-colored link?" Zamansky proposed the following changes to the activity to scaffold the discussion.

- Eliminate the staircase—the plates are connected to the floor.
- Eliminate the red dots—no hypothetical "link" between the first and last plate.
- Have students discuss with partners, then discuss with class. In the context of a class discussion, behavior of students hanging plates in different ways may be harder to interpret than written responses. (see http://secanternerve.blogspot.com)

Zamansky concludes with "Be honest with yourself. If you're not differentiating with all students, then you're not really differentiating. Every student deserves instruction matched to achieve his or her potential."

Teacher Resources for KS3 / GCSE, Year 9 / Grade 8, Problem 1

I am Pete, the editor of the NRICH website. Our slogan, 'on mathematics with attitude', means that we publish challenging problems and encourage people to think and reason for themselves about the mathematics in each situation.

We know that good problem-solving goes hand-in-hand with visualisation.

## Numbers And The Number Line

We experience mathematics almost entirely through our senses. Different people have their own ways of experiencing mathematics. Some us one sense predominantly, whereas others make sense of the world through a combination of senses.

This week we will focus on just one sense - that of sight - and we will think particularly about the representations of data, numbers and number, so let us start by thinking about things that we can see.

First of all how do we represent numbers, or data, that we encounter every day?

Here are some instances of each sense, and the corresponding representation or more formal notation:

1. Sightseeing, televisions, photographs: pictures, diagrams;
2. Hearing, music, alarms: music notation;
3. Touching, handshakes
4. taste, smells: (re)production of food and smells: recipes;
5. Thinking and understanding: language, notation.

Pictures and diagrams are a good place to start:

Here is a photograph of some coloured pebbles ;

## Visual Representations Of Facts, Data Or relationships.

• You could organise the pebbles in some way: perhaps into two piles of pebbles - organised by colour (red and blue).
You could then count how many there are in each pile (6 and 4 in this case).
• You could order them according to size, represent their weights by arranging them on the points of a balance, group them by colour, weight them and measure how many fit into 1 litre of space.

In the case of the pebbles you could relate facts in any way that you want or need.

The possibilities are endless.

### Seeing Multiplication

The most obvious representation for multiplication is that of an 'area array'

For example '3 lots of 5' can be represented by drawing a rectangular array of 3 rows and 5 columns.

## Leave the World a Better Place Through Mathematics

### The Projects

A few definitions:
Large numbers have many digits and/or involve larger-than-life numbers. They do not necessarily need to be mathematically difficult and they do not necessarily need to be done in a short period of time. (Our estimation projects also involve large numbers, because we are looking at world quantities. Estimation projects need smaller number skills for earlier grades, but we are also allowing older kids to do the projects, because they involve a lot of writing/composition as well as arithmetic and reasoning.)
Problem solving is looking beyond the obvious in a question, to try to figure out what "they're really asking." These problems require some ingenuity, but they don't have to be too difficult either.
Measurement requires the use of measurement but also a little thinking beyond the obvious. For example, "how many buses would it take to fill the Rose Bowl?", is a measurement questio because it involves figuring out how many buses would fit in a certain size area (much like figuring out how many people would fit into the same area). The difference is that the bus question requires some measurement calculations instead of kids just making an estimate.

## Teaching and Learning Issues

The standard algorithm for doing multiplication and division is both clumsy, and easy to get wrong. When multiplying multi - digit numbers we recommend pupils to use a grid method, either as a means to an end, while still learning the standard method, or as an alternative method. An image is on cards#[6]. Depending on a school's preference, the formal algorithm may be introduced early or later.

## Mental calculation

## Multiplication by 10, 100, 1000, etc

Any time you multiply by a factor of 10 (10, 100, 1000, 10,000 etc), the digits do not change, just the position of the decimal point: every factor of 10 tells you to shift the decimal place one position to the right!

The same applies if you flip the digits: if you multiply by 1/10, 1/100, 1/1000 you need to move the decimal place to the left. Two factors of 10 means moving it two places to the left, three to the right, etc.

Of course we do not usually write 2 x 10 but use the standard convention of a digit moving to the right (2 or 3 added to the power): 010 or 003 meaning 10 or 1000.

Reading response journals (daily responses to a question or selection from a novel) continue to be invaluable assessment tools in my classes. The journals are not a stressful assessment for students -- they write without regard to grades or the "right" answer. They are able to respond honestly through-out an entire novel and day-by-day for the unit. I have two more reading-response journals in store for my students. I am collecting the journals on a daily basis so that I may respond to their ideas and offer individual assistance to those students who continue to struggle.
